generation.hypothesis: The degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by the formation of stripelike elastic undulations with a characteristic wavelength of 1-2 nm, which serve as a mechanistic precursor to the formation of finely twinned microstructures, leading to catastrophic failure.

AbstractFinely twinned microstructures are widely observed in metals and alloys but the underlying formation mechanisms remain debatable. In particular, the role of internal stresses in promoting these inhomogeneous patterns is still not clear. The fracture simulation results show qualitative correspondence with the extended Rice model predictions and trends derived from experimental observations. Using pure Nb as a reference material, we identify the alloying trend that corresponds well with experimental observations and ab-initio calculations: Alloying with group IV elements decreases the GB energy and enhances ductility, whereas Group VI elements increase GB energy and promote brittleness. Atomistic-scale crack resistance curves (R-curves) and crack tip configurations reveal a near constant fracture resistance for the two nanocrystalline grain sizes explored. Compared with the averaged bulk atomistic-scale R-curves, GBs promote plastic deformation in Nb45Ta25Ti15Hf15 due to their high cohesion. Whereas in NbMoTaW, GBs promote brittle intergranular fracture except at high GB-to-crack obliquity angles where the crack is pinned temporarily to delay failure. Our findings reveal a clear mechanistic origin for the contrasting fracture behavior of brittle NbMoTaW and ductile Nb45Ta25Ti15Hf15, bridging theoretical predictions, atomistic simulations, and experimental trends.

The high entropy alloy (HEA) of equiatomic composition CrNiFeCoMn and with FCC crystal structure was additively manufactured in a selective laser melting (SLM) process starting from mechanically alloyed powders. The as-produced alloy shows fine nitride and σ phase precipitates, which are Cr-rich and stable up to about 900 K. The precipitates increase in number and dimensions after long-period annealing at 900–1300 K, with a change in the HEA mechanical properties. Higher aging temperatures in the furnace, above 1300 K, turn the alloy into a single FCC structure, with the disappearance of the nitride and σ phase precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries, but still with the presence of a finer Cr-rich nitride precipitation phase. These results suggest that the as-produced HEA is a supersaturated solid solution at low and intermediate temperature with nitrides and σ nanostructures.
